newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil minister linked to corruption scandal.
newsitem.headline: Brazil minister linked to corruption scandal.

text.p: A Brazilian corruption scandal deepened on Wednesday when a newspaper suggested a senior government minister helped buy votes for a bill that would allow President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to run for re-election.

The Folha de Sao Paulo newspaper, which on Tuesday said it had evidence five lawmakers took bribes to vote in favour of the bill, claimed it had new tapes of telephone conversations that suggested Communications Minister Sergio Motta was involved.

Motta, a close friend and business partner of the president, denied any role in the scandal. "I reject and do not recognise any of the statements transcribed in the Folha de Sao Paulo," he told reporters. "There's not one solid accusation or fact."
The minister also said he would be taking legal steps to oblige the two deputies quoted by the newspaper to either confirm or deny the comments attributed to them.

Motta's name and his nickname, Serjao, appeared several times in a transcript of the purported conversations which Folha said involved two lawmakers talking on separate occasions to an unidentified third person.

The newspaper quoted Joao Maia, a federal deputy in Brazil's Congress, as saying Motta had given money to the governor of Amazonas state, Amazonino Mendes, who paid him 200,000 reais ($188,000) for his vote.
"As far as I know it's like this. It was the 200 from Serjao via Amazonino that was the federal contribution to the agreement," the lawmaker was quoted as saying.

The re-election bill, which would allow presidents, state governors and mayors to stand for a second consecutive term, was approved in January in the Chamber of Deputies in what was considered the biggest test to date of Cardoso's administration.
The bill is now in the Senate where the first of two full votes is expected to take place next week.

Cardoso, who hopes to become Brazil's first re-elected president next year, cast doubt on the authenticity of the allegations. The deputies who were being quoted by Folha de Sao Paulo were "low-level people who don't have credibility," the president said in an interview with national Radio Eldorado.

He urged Congress to investigate quickly the reports which, he said, took him by surprise. "I followed the events with the same perplexity as the public," Cardoso said. "If the allegations are proved, immediate steps must be taken."

The scandal comes at a delicate time for Cardoso, who is trying to overcome resistance in Congress to his civil service and pension reforms. Bills to regulate the opening up of Brazil's huge telecommunications and oil industries to private competition are also awaiting approval.
Financial markets were stung by the report linking Motta to the scandal. Shares on the Sao Paulo stock exchange ended Wednesday down 3.43 percent on Wednesday.

An internal congressional inquiry was launched on Tuesday and has seven days to investigate the allegations. The probe could lead to suspension of the lawmakers involved in the alleged scam, officials said.

Left-wing oppostion parties said they were close to gathering enough signatures in the lower house to set up a wide-ranging Commission of Parliamentary Inquiry (CPI) into the scandal. They also demanded the re-election bill be put on hold.
